s.t: Andy Bell would introduce it: “When I was a little girl, I asked my mummy, ‘Can I be gay when I grow up?’ ‘Yes, if you show a little respect.’”
s.src: Yahoo Entertainment: Erasure's 'Little Respect': the story behind their 1988 hit (citing Spin, February 1989)
s.q: According to the February 1989 issue of Spin magazine, Bell, who is an openly gay man, would occasionally introduce the song by saying, "When I was a little girl, I asked my mummy, 'Can I be gay when I grow up?' She replied, 'Yes, if you show a little respect.'"

s.t: Vince Clarke told Andy Bell they couldn't call it ‘A Little Respect’, with Aretha Franklin's ‘Respect’ already out there; Bell kept the title, and calls the song “a disco hymn”.
s.q: Vince says; "oh, you can’t call it 'A Little Respect”. I said; "Vince, you can" I said; "you can call it whatever you like” , because they have R.E.S.P.E.C.T ... I love rip-roaring hymns, and to me, it’s a disco hymn.

s.t: Wheatus's 2001 cover of Erasure's ‘A Little Respect’ reached No. 3 in the UK, one place higher than Erasure's own original.
s.q: Released on 2 July 2001 by Columbia Records, it peaked at number three in the United Kingdom (besting the peak of Erasure's original)

s.t: After Hull KR fans' singing of it went viral in 2015, Andy Bell let the rugby league club's players record their own charity single of Erasure's ‘A Little Respect’.
s.q: social media videos of Hull Kingston Rovers supporters singing the song following their semi-final victory against Warrington Wolves went viral, resulting in Andy Bell granting the club's players and staff permission to record a charity single

f.t: As a teenage fan, Andy Bell practised singing along to Vince Clarke's band Yazoo; answering a Melody Maker advert for a singer, he had no idea it was Clarke's.
f.src: Yahoo Entertainment: Erasure's Vince Clarke and Andy Bell talk fateful first audition (2020)
f.q: the teenage Bell was basically a Clarke fanboy who used to practice singing to Yazoo's Upstairs at Eric's and Moyet's solo album Alf ... when he later answered an ad in the Melody Maker that read, "Established songwriter looking for versatile singer," he had no idea that the songwriter in question was his hero.

f.t: Vince Clarke later said he couldn't remember exactly why he left Depeche Mode after their first album, and that he thought he would go back to working for British Rail.
f.q: He later said he couldn't remember exactly why he left, but potentially due to ego problems, thinking he would go back to work for British Rail.

f.t: Vince Clarke was born Vincent Martin; he took the name Vince Clarke when his first band became Depeche Mode.
f.q: Clarke provided vocals until lead vocalist Dave Gahan joined the band, which was renamed Depeche Mode. At that time, he adopted the stage name Vince Clarke

f.t: Their first album, Wonderland, was a flop, which Andy Bell calls lucky: it left only one hit, ‘Oh L'amour’, to live up to.
f.q: I think we were kind of fortunate because our first album ['Wonderland', 1986] was a flop, so we only had 'Oh L'amour' [as a hit] on that album.

nf.t: Andy Bell joked his mum told him he could be gay “if you show a little respect”
nf.q: She replied, 'Yes, if you show a little respect.'
